description: We are Datanauts Brasil, a team of data professionals and a developer from São Paulo, Brazil. We turn NASA open data into clear, useful tools: from raw datasets to pipelines, analysis and interactive apps. Our motto: connecting the dots.
summary:
Every season, a farmer bets a whole year of work on one decision: what to plant next. Rain is less predictable, heat is rising, soils are tired, and a strong El Niño can wipe out a harvest. In the 2023/24 El Niño season, Brazil's grain harvest fell by about 20 million tonnes.

Rotare turns that bet into an informed choice. The farmer draws a field on a satellite map. Rotare reads more than ten years of that land from NASA satellites (crop history, rain, heat, soil moisture, slope) and recognizes the rotation already in use. The farmer says what matters most: soil, water, climate risk or income. Rotare then tests 83 three-year rotations against 30 years of real daily climate on that field's soil, including strong El Niño years.

The answer is a clear side-by-side: your current rotation versus the best alternatives, why each was suggested, its benefits, its risks and what we still don't know. On our demo field, the recommended plan raises soil health from 44 to 84 and lowers the yearly chance of crop failure from 10% to 7%.

Free NASA data, any field, in minutes. Rotare supports the farmer and the agronomist. It never replaces them.
details:
THE PROBLEM WE CARE ABOUT

Behind every field is a family deciding, season after season, what to plant next. That choice used to follow tradition and experience. Today the climate moves faster than tradition: rain arrives late, heat waves come early, soils lose organic matter, and a strong El Niño can erase a year of work. Brazil's grain harvest fell by about 20 million tonnes in the 2023/24 El Niño season, and a strong El Niño is under way again in 2026/27 (NOAA). Farmers don't need more data. They need a clear answer to one question: will my rotation hold up?

OUR SOLUTION: ROTARE

Rotare is a decision-support tool that tests crop rotations against real climate before the farmer plants, using free NASA Earth observations. It works in six simple steps:

1. Find your farm on a satellite map.

2. Draw your field. Rotare measures it precisely (WGS84).

3. Field X-ray. Rotare shows what is on the land today and more than ten years of crop history seen from space, with strong El Niño seasons highlighted. It recognizes the rotation the farmer already uses, and the farmer confirms it.

4. "The decision is yours." The farmer sets weights for soil protection, lower climate risk, water-use efficiency and profitability.

5. Rotations. Rotare tests 83 three-year combinations against 30 years of real climate, day by day, with this field's soil, and ranks them by the farmer's own priorities. The current rotation is always on screen for comparison. An El Niño mode shows how every option behaves in strong El Niño years.

6. Map. The recommended plan for the next three years, ready to discuss with the agronomist.

A REAL EXAMPLE

On our demo field ("Home Field", 317.7 ha, Sorriso, Mato Grosso), compared with the current soybean-corn rotation, the recommended "Farm balance" plan:

- raises soil health from 44 to 84;

- raises water efficiency from 45 to 100;

- lowers the yearly chance of crop failure from 10% to 7%;

- with a small, clearly shown trade-off in relative income (76 to 74).

IMPACT

Better rotations protect soil, save water and reduce losses, year after year. Because Rotare runs on free, global NASA data, the same method works for any field, from a family farm to an extension agent advising hundreds of producers. Our goal: every farm ready for the next El Niño.

CREATIVITY

Most tools tell you what to plant in an average year. Rotare is different in three ways:

- it evaluates the whole three-year sequence, not a single season;

- it starts from the rotation the farmer already uses, detected from space, so the advice is personal from the first screen;

- it stress-tests every option against real strong El Niño years, weighted by what the farmer values.

VALIDITY: HONEST BY DESIGN

- Every number shows its source, resolution and confidence.

- Each strategy explains why it was suggested, its benefits, its risks and what we don't know (for example: no lab soil test yet, market prices not included).

- El Niño mode is a scenario based on past strong El Niño years, not a weather forecast, and the app says so.

- Rotare supports local expertise. The final decision always belongs to the farmer and the agronomist.

RELEVANCE: NASA DATA AT THE CORE

Without NASA data, Rotare would not exist:

- MODIS (250 m) and HLS (30 m): ten years of crop history and bare-soil periods;

- NASA POWER: 30+ years of daily temperature for evaporation (ET0), heat and frost;

- GPM IMERG: satellite rainfall that checks the daily CHIRPS rainfall;

- SMAP: soil moisture to check the water balance;

- SRTM: slope and erosion risk.

Datasets with different resolutions are aggregated to the field the farmer draws, so every indicator describes the same piece of land.

HOW WE BUILT IT

- Web app: HTML, CSS and JavaScript with MapLibre GL (satellite globe and map) and Turf.js (geodesic area). Runs fully in the browser, works on phones, no account needed.

- Decision engine: deterministic JavaScript. A daily FAO-56 soil water balance with Hargreaves ET0 and the FAO-33 yield response simulates every crop season of the last 30 years; a soil index inspired by the USDA-NRCS Soil Conditioning Index scores cover, nutrient cycling, pests, erosion and organic matter. Covered by 19 automated tests.

- Live data for any field: a Python serverless API on Vercel reads NASA data through Google Earth Engine and the NASA POWER API in about 15 to 30 seconds.

- Data pipeline: Python (pandas, earthaccess, NASA AppEEARS, Earth Engine) saves every source as Parquet tables and a DuckDB database.

- Source code (MIT): https://github.com/GabrielHenriqueCA/field-shift-farm-insights

WHAT'S NEXT

Field validation with agronomists and cooperatives, more crops and regions, farmer lab soil tests as an input, and market prices to sharpen the income comparison.
